
## Introduction

Cortical organisation of the brain is often defined by cytoarchitecture and connectivity. Cortical regions also differ in their intrinsic activity, including their electrophysiological dynamics in the resting state. Intracranial recordings show that different brain areas have distinct spectral profiles: characteristic patterns of oscillatory peaks and broadband spectral shape that  together shape regional electrophysiological signatures [@frauscher2018AtlasNormalIntracranial; @groppe2013DominantFrequenciesResting]. Understanding of this organisation is important, as differences in regional profiles are increasingly investigated as biomarkers for early-onset and differential diagnosis of neurological and psychiatric conditions [@dekeulenaer2025DiagnosticUtilityElectrophysiological; @jaramillo-jimenez2025CharacterizingRestingstateEEG].

An important reference point for characterizing these signatures is a normative atlas of intracranial EEG published by @frauscher2018AtlasNormalIntracranial. This atlas includes 1772 channels from 106 epilepsy patients, distributed across 38 cortical regions during resting wakefulness with eyes closed. Using k-means clustering and comparison against a no-peak reference set, the authors identified region-specific patterns of oscillatory peaks across frequencies. <!-- They also characterised so non-oscillatory component of the signal using a scale-free model -->. This atlas remains one of the most comprehensive open-access resources for normative iEEG spectral features, and it provides a useful external reference for evaluating spectral maps obtained with non-invasive methods. Comparing these features across recording modalities is methodologically difficult. iEEG provides a relatively direct measure of local field potentials with limited volume conduction, making it a useful reference for regional spectral organization. In addition, iEEG has relatively clean signal: when comparing blink-related artefact amplitude with ongoing brain activity, @ball2009SignalQualitySimultaneously reported that invasive EEG/ECoG had a signal-to-noise ratio approximately 20 to more than 100 times higher than simultaneously recorded scalp EEG.

In source-reconstructed MEG, similar regional structures has  also been documented. @keitel2016IndividualHumanBrain showed that resting-state spectral profiles are distinctive enough to fingerprint individual cortical areas. @mellem2017IntrinsicFrequencyBiases found that within most regions multiple frequency bands dominate at once, so regional identity is distributed across the spectrum. @mahjoory2020FrequencyGradientHuman reported, across 187 participants, a posterior-to-anterior decrease in dominant peak frequency that anticorrelates with cortical thickness as a proxy for hierarchical level. @niso2019BrainstormPipelineAnalysis demonstrated that source-space MEG power maps of this kind are reproducible with a standardized pipeline and @shafiei2023NeurophysiologicalSignaturesCortical brought this picture even sharper linking intrinsic electrophysiological activity in MEG with cortical micro-architecture. This approach has however still some limitation, as the orginal papers discussed and @tait2021SystematicEvaluationSource shows that source reconstruction can introduce systematic distortions and variability  that propagate into spectral parameterisation.

Source-reconstructed HD-EEG is also non-invasive and provides whole-head coverage, but unlike MEG it is widely affordable: MEG offers excellent signal quality, yet most labs cannot afford it, whereas HD-EEG is comparatively cheap and routinely used. It also carries the same reconstruction caveats. Its source estimates depend on the inverse method, electrode density, head model, signal-to-noise ratio, and spatial leakage, and reconstruction can introduce spatial blurring and method-specific biases in the estimated spectral profiles  [@liu2018DetectingLargeScaleBrain; @lai2018ComparisonScalpSourcereconstructed; @piastra2020ComprehensiveStudyElectroencephalography]. Because these distortions are systematic and depend on the reconstruction pipeline, disagreement with iEEG is not straightforward evidence of failed recovery: apparent mismatches may reflect genuine modality differences, source-reconstruction artefacts, or their interaction.

A further complication is that "spectral organisation" is not a single object. Regional spectra combine narrowband peaks with broader changes in spectral shape, so apparent differences between regions or modalities can depend on which part of the spectrum is treated as oscillatory and which part as background. Under this operational view, the power spectrum can be described as a combination of narrowband rhythmic activity and a broadband, approximately $1/f^\chi$ component, whose power decreases with increasing frequency. In this chapter, terms such as "broadband background" and "aperiodic" are used in this descriptive and phenomenological  sense: they refer to the modelled broadband spectral structure that remains once clear narrowband peaks are accounted for, without assuming that it reflects a separate physiological process or saying something about its mechanism.

Classical analyses focused predominantly on oscillations, often operationalized as relative power in frequency bands,  but broadband spectral parameters also carry neurophysiological information [@donoghue2020ParameterizingNeuralPower] and show regional structure. Using other approach, @frauscher2018AtlasNormalIntracranial found regional variation in the scale-free component of intracranial EEG, including stronger scale-free values in visual regions and a low-frequency shoulder in many spectra.@armonaite2026ScaleFreeNeurodynamicsFunctional extended this line of work by showing that scale-free spectral properties can serve as regional functional fingerprints, with the high-frequency exponent distinguishing cortical from subcortical areas. Regional electrophysiological identity may therefore be expressed not only in oscillatory peaks, but also in broadband parameters such as spectral slope and offset.

At the same time, this separation remains a modelling convenience rather than a guaranteed physiological partition. As discussed in Chapter 1, the observed potential $V(t)$ is the sum of many elementary current generators, including synaptic, dendritic, and spiking contributions, each filtered by biophysical and geometric factors [@buzsaki2012OriginExtracellularFields]. Failing to model the broadband background can make differences in spectral slope appear as differences in oscillatory power; conversely, temporally varying oscillatory activity can contribute to what appears as broadband structure. The estimates themselves also depend on parameterisation choices: the exponent depends on the frequency range over which it is estimated [@gerster2022SeparatingNeuralOscillations; @boncompte2026AperiodicExponentBrain], and the choice between fixed and knee aperiodic models can change the result [@ameen2025TemporallyResolvedAnalyses].

These choices matter because periodic and aperiodic parameters are estimated jointly. Error in the fitted broadband component does not stay confined to the broadband parameters, but can propagate into the estimated rhythmic features. In simulations where periodic and aperiodic components were combined additively and left uncorrelated by construction, @castanheira2025QuantifyingRhythmicArrhythmic showed that rhythmic power estimated by detrending was highly sensitive to errors in aperiodic offset and exponent, whereas rhythmic power read from modelled spectral peaks was less contaminated. The detrending operation is also underdetermined: depending on the assumed physiological mechanism, broadband structure may relate to rhythmic peaks additively or multiplicatively, so subtraction in linear and logarithmic space imply different assumptions. This is why @brake2024NeurophysiologicalBasisAperiodic caution against detrending where clear peaks are present. A recent preprint by @bloniasz2026SpectralDecompositionsNeural makes a related point: "aperiodic broadband" may be a spectral description arising from the same additive neural generators that also produce rhythms, so decomposition methods that impose multiplicative log-power structure can misestimate both broadband slopes and oscillatory peaks.

<!-- #The present chapter uses @frauscher2018AtlasNormalIntracranial as a reference for source-reconstructed high-density EEG. 
 -->
These issues might be especially relevant for the line of cross modal validation studies. @afnan2023ValidatingMEGSource validated MEG source imaging of resting-state oscillatory patterns against the Frauscher iEEG atlas. Using 45 healthy participants and the same 38 regions of interest, they found that MEG-estimated spectra were more comparable to iEEG after aperiodic components were removed, and that lateral regions were recovered more accurately than deep or medial structures. Using different data sources, @janiukstyte2023NormativeBrainMapping presented source-localised resting-state scalp EEG maps and showed that systematic spatial variation in spectral features can be detected with scalp EEG (low-density scalp EEG vs a different iEEG reference), although with reduced spatial specificity. These studies show that regional spectral organisation can be partly preserved across modalities. 

The present chapter extends this line of work by comparing the @frauscher2018AtlasNormalIntracranial iEEG atlas with source-reconstructed HD-EEG. It first characterises the spectral structure of each dataset on its own  before asking how far these structures correspond across modalities.
The general general question is to what extent can the regional spectral organisation present in intracranial EEG be recovered in non-invasive, source-reconstructed HD-EEG, and how far does the answer depend on how narrowband (periodic) and broadband ("aperiodic") activity are operationalised? We approach it through three specific questions:

1. Before the aperiodic component is explicitly modelled and removed, what spectral structure is present in each modality, and how much of the regional structure transfers across modalities? We use two descriptors that rest on different assumptions: k-means clustering across a broad frequency range (following @frauscher2018AtlasNormalIntracranial) and per-region relative power in the traditionally defined bands.

2. When the broadband background is modelled and removed, which oscillatory features correspond across modalities — and does the choice between a detrended residual and explicitly modelled spectral peaks change that picture?

3. Are the aperiodic estimates themselves stable across the modelling and methodological choices used to obtain them — aperiodic model, fitting range, and decomposition method — so that the cross-modal comparison in (2) is reliable?

The operationalisation of oscillatory (periodic) activity has the structure of what @gelman2013GardenForkingPaths call a "garden of forking paths": multiplicity arises because several defensible analytical choices are available before the results are interpreted, not because the analyst is searching for a convenient result. Verifying if and how the cross-modal answer depends on these choices is central to this chapter but a full and exhaustive multiverse analysis (@steegen2016IncreasingTransparencyMultiverse) is outside of scope here.
